item.title: I wrote a short book about peace
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
I have published a short book on the web: The Art of Peace. Its subtitle is “On living together without thinking alike.”

The thought came to me during a morning swim in Nago Bay, in Okinawa. I was thinking about how much I love Sun Tzu’s The Art of War, and wondering what I might learn by turning the same attention to the preservation of peace. Sun Tzu’s book has thirteen chapters, and so does this one: on peace, difference, boundaries, strength, understanding, sharing, trust, diplomacy, escalation, humility, what we build, repair, and keeping peace. Each holds eight short passages, 104 in all, between an opening and a closing. The brevity comes from Sun Tzu. The warmth and the imagery I was reaching for are those of Kahlil Gibran’s The Prophet.

The peace the book describes is not agreement. As the opening puts it, “The peace I seek has room for an unwelcome answer.” It leaves people free to disagree, to change their minds, and sometimes to part. It asks restraint of those who hold power, and protection for those whose refusal would otherwise carry no weight.

I work with computers and build things, and those habits show in the pages: preparing for mistakes, keeping a failure from spreading, sharing what is useful, and making repair possible. The chapter on trust asks how promises are kept and checked between people. That is the question I usually ask of institutions and software, under the topic of trust, put to a household or a workshop instead. The chapter on sharing reads to me like a short guide to maintaining a commons: “Care for the common well includes care for those who clean it.”

This is a first manuscript, developed with AI assistance from my ideas and conversations, and it remains open to revision. The passages are principles to examine and practise, and applying them asks for judgment. You can read it in one piece, open a single chapter, or keep the Markdown copy. The book ends with the instruction I would give for anything I write: “Keep what helps. Question what does not.”

References

  • Raffael Schneider, The Art of Peace, first manuscript, 2026. Quotations are from “Before the shore”, chapter VI (“On sharing”, passage 6), and “Returning”.
  • Sun Tzu, The Art of War.
  • Kahlil Gibran, The Prophet.

item.title: One person can make a difference
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
In the early days of OpenAI, Sam Altman had a quote painted on the office walls. It comes from Hyman G. Rickover, the admiral known as the father of the nuclear navy, who built the first nuclear-powered submarines:

I believe it is the duty of each of us to act as if the fate of the world depended on him. Admittedly, one man by himself cannot do the job. However, one man can make a difference.

Karen Hao tells the story in Empire of AI (chapter 6). Years later Altman put the same quote, with a few more lines about each person’s “individual and independent capacities”, at the end of a memo to the company. The memo asked for less transparency, at least one impressive demonstration of progress a year, and more seriousness and unity. Under the quote he wrote: “We must put the mission ahead of any individual preferences.”

I like the quote, and I believe it. It is the conviction behind most things worth building, and it is the same thing I argued about who carries progress: a small number of people deciding to act as if it depends on them is how a lot of the future gets made. Rickover is a fair example. A nuclear navy was a state project, but it happened at the pace it did because one difficult man drove it.

What strikes me is the turn in the memo. Rickover’s lines are about the individual: each of us, our own capacities, our own duty. Altman uses them to ask each person to set their own judgement aside for the mission. Both can be true at once, a person can make a difference by joining something larger, but the second reading is the one that makes an organisation dangerous when the mission is as large as the one OpenAI claimed. If everyone acts as if the fate of the world depends on them, someone still has to be allowed to say that the fate of the world is not in fact at stake this quarter.

References

  • Karen Hao, Empire of AI (2025), chapter 6. Hao prints the quote with gender-neutral brackets; the wording above follows the version usually attributed to Rickover.
  • Hyman G. Rickover, attributed to “Thoughts on Man’s Purpose in Life” (1974), as given on Quotepark after Wikiquote. I have not seen the primary text.

item.title: Power, in the good sense
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
The word I have settled on for the feeling in ideas stop waiting is power. Not in the sense the word usually carries, power over someone, but in the plain sense: being capable of doing something, having possibilities, having a moat of your own. Through the AI services anyone can subscribe to, we became powerful.

It is an uncomfortable choice of word at first, and the longer I sit with it the more I like it. We have trained ourselves to hear power only as hierarchy, and to look for a victim in every arrangement that has some. This is a kind of power nobody took from anyone. It was not redistributed; it was created, and handed out to whoever cared to learn it. Capability is power, and it is a relief to say so without apology. It is the capability of one person directing many hands, which is what sixteen agents under one manager turned out to be about. What makes it more than a personal feeling is that the capability is democratised, which is where the interesting consequences start.
